# Introduction to generalized linear models {#sec-glm-intro}

```{r}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(here)

Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")
Plot_theme <- Plot_theme$value

cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))
cell_data$DPI <- as.numeric(cell_data$DPI)
```

@sec-linear-regression-multiple ended with a promise and a warning: the linear model we've been using assumes an outcome that can, in principle, take any real value, and many of the outcomes we care about can't. I made that sound abstract. It isn't. If you've ever counted cells under a microscope, you've already measured an outcome that lives in a smaller world than the whole number line, and you may have fed it to a Gaussian model without anyone telling you what that costs. This chapter is where we find out, on real counts from the dataset you already know, and then meet the machinery that fixes it.

## Cells are counted, not measured

`cell_data` has been hiding a column we haven't touched: `Pdgfrb_Pos`, the number of PDGFR-β-positive cells counted in each animal's region of interest (ROI). PDGFR-β marks pericytes and related perivascular cells, which respond to ischemic injury on a slower clock than the astrocytes we followed in the last chapter. The question is a natural companion to the tissue-area one: **how does the number of PDGFR-β+ cells change over the days after ischemia?**

Two things about how I'm treating these data, so you can hold me to them. First, there is one row per animal (49 animals, 49 rows), so I don't have a nesting problem to worry about here. Second, I'm treating the ROI as a counting window of the same size for every animal. If the window's area varied from animal to animal, a raw count would mix "more cells" with "more tissue counted", and the fix for that (an *offset*) belongs to @sec-count-regression. And because we now want the whole time course, including the sham animals at day 0, I'll treat `DPI` as a categorical predictor, exactly as in @sec-linear-regression-multiple, so each day gets its own mean and I don't have to assume a straight line through a curve I already know isn't straight.

```{r}
cell_data$DPI_f <- factor(cell_data$DPI)
```

Before any model, let's look. I want every animal visible, not a summary, because the shape of the spread is going to be the whole story. I'll mark the sham animals differently from the ischemic ones with both color and shape, since day 0 is the only day they exist.

```{r}
#| label: fig-glm_counts_by_dpi
#| fig-cap: PDGFR-$\beta$-positive cell counts per animal, by day after ischemia (day 0 is the sham group)
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false

ggplot(cell_data, aes(x = DPI_f, y = Pdgfrb_Pos)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = Condition, shape = Condition),
              width = 0.12, size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.5,
               linewidth = 0.4, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(SHAM = "#D55E00", MCAO = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "PDGFR-β+ cells in the ROI") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Two things jump out, and I'd like you to notice them before I name them. On days 0 and 3 the counts sit low, around 500, in a fairly tight cluster pressed against the floor of the plot. From day 7 they climb to two or three thousand and *fan out*: the animals on day 7 differ from each other by more than the entire day-3 group's range. The floor is a zero you can't go below; the fan is a spread that grows with the mean. A count has both of those properties, always. Keep them in mind while we try the model we already know.

## First attempt: pretend it's Gaussian

I could tell you why a Gaussian is a bad idea for counts, and you'd nod. I'd rather show you, because seeing a model fail on your own data teaches more than being warned about it. So here is the straight linear model, one mean per day and one common `sigma`, fit the way every model in the last three chapters was: with the flat `brms` defaults, so the data speak with as little interference as possible, and beside its `lm` counterpart.

```{r}
library(brms)

fit_gauss <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/glm-intro_fit1.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_gauss)
```

The `Intercept` is the day-0 mean (about 513 cells) and each `DPI_f` coefficient is how far that day sits from it, just like the categorical predictor in @sec-linear-regression-multiple. Sampling is healthy, and the means themselves are perfectly reasonable summaries. The trouble is `sigma`: a single number, around 700, meant to describe how far an animal typically sits from its day's mean.

### parsnip

```{r}
library(parsnip)
library(broom)

parsnip_gauss <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data)

tidy(parsnip_gauss, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

The coefficients aren't wrong. What a model *believes* about the world lives in the data it would simulate, and that's what @sec-mcmc-model-checking taught us to check. So let's ask the model to generate fake animals, day by day, and see whether they look like real counts. I'm using `posterior_predict()` to draw new observations (not just new means) and `ggdist`'s graded intervals to show where the model thinks a new animal would land, with the real animals on top and a dashed line at zero.

```{r}
#| label: fig-glm_gauss_predictive
#| fig-cap: Where the Gaussian model expects a new animal's count to fall on each day (bands are 50%, 80% and 95% predictive intervals), against the observed animals
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false

library(ggdist)

pp_gauss <- posterior_predict(fit_gauss, ndraws = 1000)

pp_long <- data.frame(
  y = as.vector(pp_gauss),
  DPI_f = rep(cell_data$DPI_f, each = nrow(pp_gauss))
)

ggplot(pp_long, aes(x = DPI_f, y = y)) +
  stat_interval(.width = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30") +
  geom_point(data = cell_data, aes(y = Pdgfrb_Pos),
             color = "black", size = 1.6, alpha = 0.7,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Blues", name = "Predictive\ninterval") +
  labs(x = "Days post-ischemia (DPI)", y = "PDGFR-β+ cells in the ROI") +
  Plot_theme
```

```{r}
neg_share <- tapply(colMeans(pp_gauss < 0), cell_data$DPI_f, mean)
```

On days 0 and 3 the bands spill below zero: the model thinks there is a `r round(100 * neg_share["0"])`% chance that a new day-0 animal has a *negative* number of cells, and about `r round(100 * neg_share["3"])`% for day 3. Nobody has ever counted minus three hundred pericytes. And notice the second problem, which you've met before: the bands are exactly as wide on day 3 as on day 7, because there is only one `sigma`. The real animals disagree. The standard deviation of the counts runs from about 190 cells on day 0 to over 900 on day 7. This is the same complaint @sec-linear-regression-multiple ended on, a single `sigma` that's too generous for the tight groups and too stingy for the loose ones, only now the tight groups are pushed against a wall.

One quieter thing before we move on: the *means* stayed sensible. The Gaussian's failure is in what it thinks is possible around them, in the predictions and the uncertainty, which is exactly where it would hurt you if you reported an interval for a new animal, or trusted the standard errors on the low-count days.

## What a GLM actually is

Here's the way I like to think about the fix. Suppose you do your arithmetic in a room with no walls: any number, positive or negative, is fine, and adding one thing to another always makes sense. That's where the linear predictor lives, the part you already know: $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots$. Now suppose the quantity you actually care about (the expected count) lives in a smaller room, one that only admits valid values. You need a doorway between the two rooms: something that takes whatever number the linear predictor produces and translates it into a value the small room accepts. And you need to say what kind of noise the outcome has once you're in the small room, because a count is noisy in a different way than a tissue area. A generalized linear model is exactly those three choices, made explicitly [@mcelreath2020; @inchausti2023]:

1. **A family**: the probability distribution that describes the scatter of the outcome around its mean. (Gaussian, Poisson, binomial, and others.)
2. **A linear predictor** $\eta_i$: the additive combination of predictors you already know how to write.
3. **A link function** $g$: the doorway. It connects the mean of the outcome, $\mu_i$, to the linear predictor.

$$
y_i \sim \text{Family}(\mu_i, \dots), \qquad g(\mu_i) = \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \dots + \beta_k x_{ki}
$$ {#eq-glm}

Read the second half in both directions. The link $g$ takes the mean to the unbounded scale; its inverse $g^{-1}$ takes the linear predictor back to a valid mean, $\mu_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i)$. Software does the second one whenever it predicts.

That's a lot of new vocabulary for something you've been doing since @sec-linear-regression-what. The reassuring part: **everything you've fit so far is already a GLM.** A Gaussian family with the *identity* link ($g(\mu) = \mu$, the doorway that changes nothing) is @eq-linear-regression-simple, with no new machinery at all. The reason we never needed a doorway is that a Gaussian mean is allowed to be any real number, so the unbounded room and the small room were the same room. Counts and proportions aren't so lucky. Here is what the doorways look like.

```{r}
#| label: fig-glm_links
#| fig-cap: Three inverse links, each translating an unbounded linear predictor into a valid mean
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
#| warning: false

eta <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 200)

links <- rbind(
  data.frame(eta = eta, mu = eta, link = "Identity"),
  data.frame(eta = eta, mu = exp(eta), link = "Log (inverse: exp)"),
  data.frame(eta = eta, mu = plogis(eta), link = "Logit (inverse: logistic)")
)
links$link <- factor(links$link, levels = unique(links$link))

ggplot(links, aes(x = eta, y = mu)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_line(color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~link, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Linear predictor (η)", y = "Mean on the outcome scale (μ)") +
  Plot_theme
```

I drew the dashed zero line in every panel on purpose. In the first panel, the line crosses it: a Gaussian model with an identity link will cheerfully predict negative values if the linear predictor goes there. In the second, the exponential curve approaches zero forever and never crosses it, so no matter how negative $\eta$ gets, $\mu = e^{\eta}$ stays positive. That's the doorway for counts. In the third, the logistic curve squeezes the whole real line into the interval between 0 and 1, which is the doorway for proportions (and, next chapter but one, for yes/no outcomes). The families and links this book will use, and where they show up, are collected below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-glm_families
#| tbl-cap: The families and links this book uses, and where each appears

library(gt)

families <- data.frame(
  Outcome = c("Continuous, unbounded", "Yes/no, or successes out of trials", "Counts",
              "Continuous proportion in (0, 1)", "Continuous with heavy tails",
              "Ordered categories"),
  Family = c("Gaussian", "Binomial", "Poisson / negative binomial",
             "Beta", "Student-t", "Cumulative"),
  Link = c("Identity", "Logit", "Log", "Logit", "Identity", "Logit"),
  Chapter = c("Linear regression chapters", "Logistic regression", "Count regression",
              "Beta and robust regression", "Beta and robust regression",
              "Ordinal regression (planned)")
)

gt(families)
```

::: callout-tip
### Don't pick the family by staring at a histogram

It's tempting to look at the shape of the outcome's histogram and choose a family to match. McElreath's name for this is "histomancy", and his objection is that it's the wrong evidence [@mcelreath2020]. What decides the family is what the outcome *is*: a number of cells is a whole number that can't go below zero; a number of successes out of a known number of trials can't exceed the trials. Those facts constrain the family before you've looked at a single value. The histogram of the raw outcome also pools animals from different conditions, so it can look lumpy or smooth for reasons that have nothing to do with the family.
:::

## Same question, new clothes: Poisson with a log link

The smallest change that respects what a count *is* is to swap the family for the Poisson, the distribution for counts of independent events at a steady rate, and the link for the log. That's it: same formula, same predictor, two changes. In `brms` it's one argument.

```{r}
fit_pois <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data,
  family = poisson(),
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/glm-intro_fit2.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_pois)
```

### glm

```{r}
glm_pois <- glm(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f, family = poisson(), data = cell_data)

tidy(glm_pois, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

Read these coefficients carefully, because they're not on the scale you're used to. They're on the *link* scale, the log scale. The `Intercept` of about 6.24 is $\log(\mu)$ for day 0, so the expected day-0 count is $e^{6.24} \approx 513$, the same mean the Gaussian gave. The `DPI_f7` coefficient of about 1.43 isn't "1.43 more cells", it's "1.43 more on the log scale", and adding on the log scale means multiplying on the count scale: $e^{1.43} \approx 4.2$, so day 7 has about four times as many PDGFR-β+ cells as day 0. It's the same kind of arithmetic as pH, where each unit is a factor of ten rather than a fixed amount. This is the price of the doorway: you can't read a coefficient off the summary and add it to a count anymore, you have to translate through the inverse link. What you gain is that the model can never predict fewer than zero cells. And, as a bonus, effects on the ratio scale ("four times as many") are usually the honest way to describe how cell counts change anyway.

::: callout-warning
### A word about priors on the link scale

I'm using the `brms` defaults again, for the same reason as before: I want the coefficients to reflect the data while we learn the structure. But this is where a habit from Gaussian models can hurt you. On the log scale, a prior that looks timid, like a Normal with a standard deviation of 10 on a coefficient, is not vague on the count scale: it says a change of 20 log-units is plausible, which is a factor of hundreds of millions. Priors on link-scale coefficients need to be judged by what they imply on the *outcome* scale, which @sec-priors-regularization taught you to do with a prior predictive check.
:::

The floor problem is gone. What about the fan? Let's find out whether the Poisson family's *own* idea of how variance should behave matches the data. A Poisson count has one defining property: its variance equals its mean. Here are the two side by side, one point per day, on log axes, with the variance each family says a group should have.

```{r}
#| label: fig-glm_mean_variance
#| fig-cap: Variance against mean for each day's counts (points), and the variance each family assumes (lines). Both axes are logarithmic.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| warning: false

day_stats <- aggregate(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data,
                       FUN = function(x) c(m = mean(x), v = var(x)))
day_stats <- do.call(data.frame, day_stats)
names(day_stats) <- c("DPI_f", "m", "v")

sigma_gauss <- summary(fit_gauss)$spec_pars["sigma", "Estimate"]
mu_grid <- exp(seq(log(350), log(4000), length.out = 100))

var_lines <- data.frame(
  mu = mu_grid,
  Poisson = mu_grid,
  Gaussian = sigma_gauss^2
)
var_lines <- rbind(
  data.frame(mu = var_lines$mu, v = var_lines$Poisson, family = "Poisson"),
  data.frame(mu = var_lines$mu, v = var_lines$Gaussian, family = "Gaussian")
)

line_labels <- var_lines[var_lines$mu == max(var_lines$mu), ]

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = var_lines, aes(x = mu, y = v, color = family, linetype = family),
            linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = line_labels, aes(x = mu, y = v, label = family, color = family),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  geom_point(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v), size = 3, color = "black") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v, label = paste("DPI", DPI_f)),
                  size = 3, min.segment.length = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 4000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
                expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.3))) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Poisson = "#D55E00", Gaussian = "grey40")) +
  labs(x = "Mean of the day's counts", y = "Variance of the day's counts") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The Gaussian says the variance should be the same no matter the mean: that's the flat grey line, and the points refuse to lie on it. The Poisson says the variance should equal the mean: the orange diagonal. The points *do* climb with the mean, so the Poisson has the right instinct, but they sit one to two orders of magnitude above the line: the day-7 group has a variance near 850,000 where a Poisson expects about 2,100. The standard summary is the *dispersion statistic*, the sum of squared Pearson residuals divided by the residual degrees of freedom, which should be near 1 for a well-specified Poisson [@inchausti2023; @gelman2020].

```{r}
dispersion <- function(m) sum(residuals(m, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m)
disp_pois <- dispersion(glm_pois)
```

Ours is about `r round(disp_pois)`. To see what that means for the predictions, I'll do what we did for the Gaussian: ask the fitted model to generate data and compare. This time I'm using `pp_check()`, and truncating the axis at 6,000 because a few Poisson replicates wander out further than any real animal.

```{r}
#| label: fig-glm_pois_ppcheck
#| fig-cap: Posterior predictive check for the Poisson model. The observed counts (dark line) are far more spread out than any replicate (light lines).
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false

pp_check(fit_pois, ndraws = 50) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6000))
```

The replicates (light lines) are lumpy little spikes, one per day, because the model believes each day's counts cluster tightly around their mean. The observed density (dark line) is a single broad plateau. The Poisson family fixed the floor and got the direction of the variance right, and it is still off by a factor of hundreds, which means every interval it reports would be wildly too narrow. A GLM isn't a spell: it gives you a family, and if the family's idea of noise is wrong, the model is wrong, just in a more respectable-looking way.

## A Poisson that works: change one word

So here is the question you asked me, and it's the right one: can a count model fail and then, with a small change, work? Yes. And the change is the whole point of having a *framework* instead of a menu of separate techniques.

Why is the Poisson too tight? Think about what it assumes. It describes what you'd see if every animal in a group had the same true density of PDGFR-β+ cells and the only randomness was which cells happened to fall inside your counting window. But animals aren't identical. Some mice just have more pericytes in that patch of tissue than others, before you ever count anything. So your count is noisy twice: once because you sampled a window, and again because the *underlying rate* itself differs from animal to animal. The Poisson has room for the first kind of noise and none for the second.

The **negative binomial** family adds exactly that second source. It is a Poisson whose rate varies from animal to animal, and it does so with one extra parameter that lets the variance exceed the mean: $\text{Var}(y) = \mu + \mu^2/\phi$, where a larger $\phi$ means less extra scatter, and $\phi \to \infty$ gives the Poisson back [@inchausti2023]. Same linear predictor, same log link. In `brms`, the change is one word.

```{r}
fit_nb <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data,
  family = negbinomial(),
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/glm-intro_fit3.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_nb)
```

### glm.nb

```{r}
glm_nb <- MASS::glm.nb(Pdgfrb_Pos ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data)

tidy(glm_nb, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

The coefficient table looks almost the same as the Poisson's: the same log-scale means, the same fourfold jump at day 7. That's the point: the *mean model* didn't change. What changed is `shape` (the $\phi$ above), which the Poisson didn't have, and which is now estimated to be around `r round(summary(fit_nb)$spec_pars["shape", "Estimate"], 1)`: small enough that the extra variance is substantial. Now the same check as before, side by side with the Poisson.

```{r}
#| label: fig-glm_ppcheck_compare
#| fig-cap: Posterior predictive checks for the Poisson (left) and negative binomial (right) models
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| warning: false

library(patchwork)

p_pois <- pp_check(fit_pois, ndraws = 50) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6000)) +
  labs(title = "Poisson")

p_nb <- pp_check(fit_nb, ndraws = 50) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6000)) +
  labs(title = "Negative binomial")

p_pois + p_nb
```

Now the replicates are broad enough to cover the observed density instead of ignoring it. They aren't perfect: their right tail reaches past 6,000, further than any animal we counted, so the negative binomial is slightly generous with the high counts. That's a much smaller sin than being off by a factor of hundreds. And the mean-variance picture finally has a curve that runs through the points. I'm adding the negative binomial's variance function, $\mu + \mu^2/\phi$, to the same plot as before.

```{r}
#| label: fig-glm_mean_variance_nb
#| fig-cap: The same variance-against-mean plot, now with the negative binomial's variance function
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| warning: false

shape_nb <- summary(fit_nb)$spec_pars["shape", "Estimate"]

var_lines_nb <- rbind(
  var_lines,
  data.frame(mu = mu_grid, v = mu_grid + mu_grid^2 / shape_nb,
             family = "Negative binomial")
)
line_labels_nb <- var_lines_nb[var_lines_nb$mu == max(var_lines_nb$mu), ]

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = var_lines_nb, aes(x = mu, y = v, color = family, linetype = family),
            linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = line_labels_nb, aes(x = mu, y = v, label = family, color = family),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  geom_point(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v), size = 3, color = "black") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = day_stats, aes(x = m, y = v, label = paste("DPI", DPI_f)),
                  size = 3, min.segment.length = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 4000), labels = scales::label_comma(),
                expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.4))) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Poisson = "#D55E00", Gaussian = "grey40",
                                "Negative binomial" = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Mean of the day's counts", y = "Variance of the day's counts") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Strictly speaking, the negative binomial isn't "a Poisson that works": it's a different family. But nothing else in the model moved: the predictor, the log link, the formula, the way we read coefficients. That's what "generalized" buys you. The choice of noise is a dial you turn independently of the rest.

Since the log link now gives us trustworthy uncertainty, let's finally read the effect the way it deserves to be read: as a ratio. Each `DPI_f` coefficient exponentiates to a fold change relative to day 0. A half-eye shows the whole posterior for each ratio, not just an interval, on a log axis so that "twice as many" and "half as many" are the same distance from 1.

```{r}
#| label: fig-glm_fold_change
#| fig-cap: Posterior fold change in PDGFR-$\beta$+ cell count relative to day 0 (negative binomial model). The dashed line at 1 means no change.
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| warning: false

draws_nb <- as.data.frame(posterior::as_draws_df(fit_nb))
day_cols <- c("b_DPI_f3", "b_DPI_f7", "b_DPI_f14", "b_DPI_f30")

fold <- data.frame(
  day = factor(rep(c(3, 7, 14, 30), each = nrow(draws_nb)), levels = c(30, 14, 7, 3)),
  fold_change = exp(unlist(draws_nb[, day_cols]))
)

ggplot(fold, aes(x = fold_change, y = day)) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.5, 0.95), fill = "#0072B2", point_interval = "median_qi") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16)) +
  labs(x = "Fold change in PDGFR-β+ cells vs. day 0 (log scale)",
       y = "Days post-ischemia") +
  Plot_theme
```

Day 3 straddles the dashed line: no detectable change from the day-0 baseline. Then day 7 jumps to roughly four times baseline, day 14 to roughly six times, and day 30 comes back down a little, to about four. That's a delayed surge, which makes biological sense for cells that respond to injury after the acute phase is over, and it's a very different picture from the "no change" a low-count Gaussian's overconfident intervals would have hidden. One caution about the reference point: day 0 is the sham group, so every one of these fold changes compares an ischemic animal at some time point to a sham animal. It cannot separate the effect of the ischemia from the effect of the passage of time, because there are no sham animals at later days (the design limit we met in @sec-linear-regression-multiple).

## The same idea for proportions

`cell_data` gives us a second way to look at the same cells. `Pdgfrb_Total` is the total number of cells counted in the ROI and `Pdgfrb_Pos` is how many of those were PDGFR-β-positive, so the natural quantity for a different question ("what *fraction* of the cells I counted are positive?") is a proportion. (There's also a `Pdgfrb_Neg` column, and where it's present, `Pos + Neg = Total` exactly. One animal, Td79, has an empty `Neg`, and its `Total` was computed as if that gap were zero, so for that animal `Pos` equals `Total` and its proportion is exactly 1, an artifact of the gap rather than a measurement; @sec-eda-missing-data tells the story. `Pos` and `Total` are complete, so I use those two, and I keep Td79 in as one animal out of 49, but remember it when a single proportion looks too perfect.)

A proportion built from a known number of trials has its own family, the **binomial**, and its own link, the **logit**, which is the third doorway in @fig-glm_links. Every step is the same as before: choose a family, choose a link, keep the linear predictor. `brms` writes the trials into the formula.

```{r}
fit_binom <- brm(
  Pdgfrb_Pos | trials(Pdgfrb_Total) ~ DPI_f,
  data = cell_data,
  family = binomial(),
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/glm-intro_fit4.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
summary(fit_binom)
```

### glm

```{r}
glm_binom <- glm(cbind(Pdgfrb_Pos, Pdgfrb_Total - Pdgfrb_Pos) ~ DPI_f,
                 family = binomial(), data = cell_data)

tidy(glm_binom, conf.int = TRUE)
```
:::

The coefficients are now log-odds, a scale that deserves its own chapter, and @sec-logistic-regression gives it one. For now, all you need is the direction: the intercept (about $-0.67$) corresponds to a day-0 proportion near one third positive, and every later day is higher, with day 14 at nearly 85%. The doorway is doing its job: whatever the linear predictor says, the fitted proportion stays between 0 and 1.

So does this family have the right idea about noise? Same question, same suspicion. The binomial says the scatter of a proportion around its mean depends on how many cells were counted and nothing else. To check, I'll ask the model where it expects each animal's proportion to land, and see whether the observed proportions honor that.

```{r}
#| label: fig-glm_binom_check
#| fig-cap: Observed proportion of PDGFR-$\beta$+ cells per animal (points) against the binomial model's 95% predictive interval for that animal (grey bars). Animals outside their interval are marked with a triangle.
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| warning: false

yrep <- posterior_predict(fit_binom, ndraws = 1000)
prop_rep <- sweep(yrep, 2, cell_data$Pdgfrb_Total, "/")

check <- cell_data[, c("DPI_f", "Pdgfrb_Pos", "Pdgfrb_Total")]
check$obs <- check$Pdgfrb_Pos / check$Pdgfrb_Total
check$lo <- apply(prop_rep, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025)
check$hi <- apply(prop_rep, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975)
check$outside <- check$obs < check$lo | check$obs > check$hi
check <- check[order(check$DPI_f, check$obs), ]
check$idx <- seq_len(nrow(check))

ggplot(check, aes(x = idx)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), color = "grey70", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = obs, color = outside, shape = outside), size = 2.2) +
  facet_grid(~DPI_f, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x",
             labeller = labeller(DPI_f = function(x) paste("DPI", x))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#0072B2", "TRUE" = "#D55E00"), guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("FALSE" = 16, "TRUE" = 17), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Animals, grouped by day", y = "Proportion PDGFR-β+") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
```

```{r}
disp_binom <- dispersion(glm_binom)
share_outside <- mean(check$outside)
```

The bars are very narrow, because with hundreds or thousands of cells counted per animal, a binomial thinks a proportion should be pinned down almost exactly. The animals don't cooperate: `r round(100 * share_outside)`% of them fall outside their 95% interval, where about 5% should, and the dispersion statistic is about `r round(disp_binom)` against an ideal of 1. It's the same story as the counts, told in a different family: the binomial has no room for animal-to-animal differences in the underlying proportion, and there are plenty. The remedy is again a change of family, to one that lets the proportion itself vary across animals, and it comes with the rest of the toolkit for proportions in @sec-logistic-regression and @sec-beta-robust-regression.

## Can we trust the sampling?

Four `brms` fits went by in this chapter, and I commented on the sampler for only the first. Since the whole argument here rests on comparing models (Gaussian against Poisson against negative binomial), I'd like to know that each one explored its posterior properly before I compare what they believe. One table covers all four, using the thresholds from @sec-mcmc-model-checking: Rhat below 1.01, both effective sample sizes above 400, and no divergent transitions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-glm_mcmc
#| tbl-cap: MCMC diagnostics for every model fitted in this chapter

source("functions/mcmc_check.R")

glm_checks <- mcmc_check(list(
  "Gaussian" = fit_gauss,
  "Poisson" = fit_pois,
  "Negative binomial" = fit_nb,
  "Binomial" = fit_binom
))
stopifnot(all(glm_checks$ok))

gt(glm_checks) |>
  fmt_number(columns = max_rhat, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(min_ess_bulk, min_ess_tail), decimals = 0)
```

All four pass: the worst Rhat is `r sprintf("%.3f", max(glm_checks$max_rhat))`, the smallest effective sample size is `r round(min(glm_checks$min_ess_bulk, glm_checks$min_ess_tail))`, and there are `r sum(glm_checks$divergences)` divergent transitions. So the differences we saw between families come from the families themselves, not from a sampler that gave up halfway.

## Modeling more than the mean

Step back and notice what changed across this chapter, and what didn't. The *mean* model, one mean per day, stayed almost exactly the same throughout. What kept changing was the family, which is a statement about the noise: how much scatter to expect, and how that scatter depends on the mean. The Gaussian said "the same everywhere". The Poisson said "as big as the mean". The negative binomial said "bigger than the mean, and growing with it". Choosing a family is choosing a model for the variance, and in every case here it was the variance, not the mean, that broke first.

That's the same lesson @sec-linear-regression-multiple ended on, seen from a different side. There, a single `sigma` was too stingy for day 3 and too generous for days 7 and 14, and I told you the fix was to model `sigma` itself as a function of the predictor. A GLM's family already does a version of that, automatically, by tying the variance to the mean. The negative binomial still has one `shape` for every day, so it isn't the full answer: @sec-multivariate-distributional-regression lets that parameter depend on predictors too. But the logic is the same. A regression is not only a model for where the middle of the data sits; it can be a model for how the whole distribution behaves, and the GLM is the first place where that becomes visible.

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

`glm()` and `MASS::glm.nb()` fit the same models by maximum likelihood, and they land close to `brms` for the same reason as in earlier chapters: with flat default priors, the posterior is shaped almost entirely by the likelihood [@gelman2020]. You can see it in the numbers: the day-7 log-scale coefficient is `r round(coef(glm_nb)["DPI_f7"], 2)` in `glm.nb` and `r round(fixef(fit_nb)["DPI_f7", "Estimate"], 2)` in `brms`. The two philosophies would start to disagree where the data are thin relative to the model. Day 0 has only seven animals, and the negative binomial's dispersion parameter is estimated from so few animals per group that a frequentist fit can become unstable, while a weakly informative prior on `shape` would keep it in a sensible range. With a link function, there's one more difference worth carrying forward: intervals for the coefficients are (roughly) symmetric on the *link* scale, so on the count scale they become asymmetric ratios, and they are only trustworthy if the family's variance assumption holds, which is why the checks in this chapter mattered more than the coefficient tables.
:::

## Where this leaves us

We started with a simple question about counting cells and found that the tool from the last four chapters couldn't answer it honestly. A Gaussian model on counts predicts impossible values and one spread for every group. A GLM is the general fix: a family for the noise, a linear predictor you already know, and a link that translates between them. The Poisson with a log link kept counts positive and still underestimated the noise by two orders of magnitude, and a negative binomial with the same link and the same formula got it right. The binomial with a logit link repeated the same lesson for proportions, and it's waiting for the same kind of rescue.

None of that machinery has been unpacked yet, and that's what the next two chapters do. @sec-logistic-regression takes the logit link on its own terms: what log-odds mean, how to read them, and how to report them to a reader who has never met one. @sec-count-regression returns to the counts, with a closer look at the negative binomial, at what to do when the counting window isn't the same size for every animal, and at the excess zeros that spike counts, unlike these, are known for.
